slides.label: LO5 statement
slides.notes: Read it out. The emphasis is recognise - reading a chart and reading the sky, not forecasting.
slides.html:
Learning Outcome 5
Be able to recognise weather conditions that affect land navigation

slides.label: Section: air masses
slides.notes: Signpost. The idea to land first is that weather arrives from somewhere, and where it came from tells you what it will do.
slides.html:
Part One
Air masses
Six of them reach the British Isles. Each one arrives with its own weather.

slides.label: Global circulation
slides.notes: Keep it to the simple convection story - rises at the equator, sinks at the poles. The complications are worth naming but not explaining; the outcome only needs the pattern.
slides.html:
Air masses
The engine is the equator
Air moves across the planet in a pattern, and the whole system is driven by the equator being the hottest part of the Earth.
▸The sun heats the surface unevenly.
▸Warm air rises over the equator and flows at height towards the poles.
▸Cold air sinks at the poles and flows back along the surface.
▸Approaching the poles there is less room, so some air is squeezed down and mixes at lower levels.
▸Add the spin of the Earth and it complicates further.
Warm air rises at the equator, cold air sinks at the poles

slides.label: The six air masses
slides.notes: Point out the arrow widths - polar maritime is by far the most common visitor. Ask them to predict from the names alone whether each one will be warm or cold, wet or dry; maritime means wet and continental means dry.

slides.label: Arctic maritime
slides.notes: The navigation consequence is what matters: snow showers and low cloud on high ground. Ask what that does to their ability to set a map on features.

slides.label: Polar continental
slides.notes: The sea-track idea is the transferable one: the same air arrives dry in the south and showery in the east purely because of how much sea it crossed. Cold and clear is good for navigation but hard on cadets.

slides.label: Tropical continental
slides.notes: The navigation point is the poor visibility, which surprises cadets who assume hot means clear. Heat plus haze on a summer exercise means fewer distant features to work from.

slides.label: Tropical maritime
slides.notes: This is the classic British murk and the worst air mass for hill navigation - low cloud, drizzle, hill fog, no visible features. Note the lee-side clearance; it explains why one side of a range is in cloud and the other is not.

slides.label: Returning polar maritime
slides.notes: The one cadets find fiddly because it is the same air as polar maritime with a different history. Dry but grey is the summary.

slides.label: Polar maritime
slides.notes: The most likely air mass on any given exercise, so know it best. The summer-winter reversal is worth explaining: in winter the sea is warmer than the land, in summer the land is warmer, and the showers follow the heat.

slides.label: Section: charts
slides.notes: Signpost. By the end of this section they should be able to look at a chart and say whether tomorrow is navigable.
slides.html:
Part Two
Weather charts
What all those lines and symbols actually tell you.

slides.label: What is on the map
slides.notes: Use this as the map of the section rather than explaining anything yet. Get cadets to point at each item on the chart as you name it.
slides.html:
Weather charts
What is on the map
Everything on this chart gets a slide of its own.
▸Low pressure region
▸High pressure region
▸Trough and ridge
▸Col
▸Cold front
▸Warm front
▸Occluded front
▸Isobars
One chart, nine things to read off it

slides.label: Lows and highs
slides.notes: Drill the two rotation directions until they are automatic - it is the most examinable fact in the section. The winter fog under a high catches cadets out, who assume high pressure always means good weather.
slides.html:
Weather charts
Lows and highs
The two features that organise everything else on the chart.
▸Depression, or low — closely spaced isobars, roughly circular, pressure lower than around it. Winds blow anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere. Lowest pressure at the centre. Strong winds, heavy rain, nearly always with fronts.
▸Anticyclone, or high — a large area of widely spaced isobars, pressure higher than around it. Winds blow clockwise. Highest pressure at the centre. Warm and sunny in summer; cold and foggy in winter.
Anticlockwise round a low, clockwise round a high

slides.label: Troughs ridges cols
slides.notes: The contour comparison does the teaching here, and it links straight back to LO1. Cadets who can read a re-entrant can read a trough.
slides.html:
Weather charts
Troughs, ridges and cols
▸Trough — an elongated extension of low pressure. Brings weather like a depression.
▸Ridge — an elongated extension of high pressure. Brings weather like an anticyclone.
▸Col — an area of slack pressure between two highs and two lows.
The contour parallel
Isobars behave like contour lines. A trough is a valley of pressure, a ridge is a spur, a col is a saddle — the same words for the same shapes.

slides.label: Fronts
slides.notes: Teach the symbols by which way they point, because that is how you read the direction of travel off a chart. The practical sequence for a walker is rain, then mild murk, then a sharp burst and clearance.
slides.html:
Weather charts
Fronts
A front is a boundary where one air mass replaces another.
▸Cold front — bold line with triangles, blue on colour charts. The points show the direction of travel. Warmer air being replaced by colder. Short spells of heavy showery rain, squally winds, a drop in temperature, wind veering, then brighter showery conditions.
▸Warm front — bold line with semicircles or humps, red on colour charts. The humps show the direction of travel. Colder air being replaced by warmer. Prolonged, sometimes heavy rain with strong winds.
▸Warm sector — between the warm front and the cold front. Mild, but often overcast with drizzle.

slides.label: Isobars
slides.notes: Spacing equals wind strength is the single most useful thing on the chart for a hill day. Get them to compare two areas of a real chart and say which one they would rather be walking in.
slides.html:
Weather charts
Isobars, pressure and wind
Isobars join points of equal pressure — contour lines for the atmosphere, drawn every 4 millibars.
▸Values are corrected to mean sea level first, so altitude does not distort the map.
▸Close together — strong winds. Near a depression, for example.
▸Widely spaced — light winds. Near an anticyclone.
▸Wind blows almost parallel to the isobars.
▸Round a high it blows slightly outward across them; into a low, slightly inward.
Isobar spacing is wind strength

slides.label: Buys Ballots Law
slides.notes: Do it outside if there is any wind at all - it takes ten seconds and it is memorable. Then ask what it tells them about whether the weather is improving or deteriorating.
slides.html:
Weather charts
Buys Ballot’s Law
Stand with your back to the wind in the northern hemisphere and low pressure is on your left.
▸Which means you can work out the wind direction anywhere on a chart.
▸Or, standing outside, work out roughly where the low is.
▸A free orientation check that needs no instrument at all.
Back to the wind — low pressure on your left

slides.label: Depression chart
slides.notes: This slide is where the abstraction becomes real. Get them to trace the fronts on the satellite image before you point them out on the chart.
slides.html:
Weather charts
Satellite and chart together
The same storm seen from space and drawn as a chart
The spiral of cloud in the satellite image is the same thing as the circle of isobars on the chart.

slides.label: Fronts cross section
slides.notes: The steepness difference explains the weather: a gentle warm front gives hours of steady rain, a steep cold front gives a short violent burst. Occlusion is the end of the depression, not the start.
slides.html:
Fronts
In cross section
Where a cold air mass meets a warm one they do not mix. The warm air rides up over the cold, pressure drops, and cold air rushes in to fill the gap.
▸That produces the spiralling motion into the centre of the depression — always anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere.
▸Note the cold front is steeper than the warm front.
▸As the depression travels, the wedge of warm air travels with it.
▸The cold front moves slightly faster, so it catches up.
▸Cold air slides under the warm air completely — a continuous cold layer at ground level with warm air on top.
▸That is an occluded front, and usually a sign the depression is filling up.
The cold front is steeper than the warm front

slides.label: Section: clouds
slides.notes: Signpost. Frame cloud reading as the skill that works without any equipment, which makes it the most useful thing in the outcome.
slides.html:
Part Three
Clouds
Three families, three levels, and ten names. What is above you tells you what is coming.

slides.label: Three families three levels
slides.notes: Establish the three levels before the names, because the prefixes cirro and alto are just level labels. Once they see that, ten cloud names collapse into three families times three heights.
slides.html:
Clouds
Three families, three levels
Cloud forms mostly in the troposphere, which runs from sea level to about 33,000 feet. When air cools past its saturation point, the vapour condenses.
▸High — 16,500 to 45,000 feet
▸Middle — 6,500 to 23,000 feet
▸Low — 0 to 6,500 feet
▸The three major types are cirrus, stratus and cumulus.
Why the troposphere
That is where the water vapour is. No vapour, no cloud.

slides.label: Cirrus stratus cumulus
slides.notes: Give them the shape words: wispy, layered, heaped. If a cadet can sort any cloud into one of those three by shape alone, they can name it with the height prefix.
slides.html:
Clouds
The three families
High
Cirrus
White, delicate filaments — horse tails or wispy strands. Cirrus, cirrocumulus, cirrostratus. 16,500–45,000 ft.
Layered
Stratus
A grey layer with a fairly uniform base. May give drizzle, snow or snow grains. Stratus, stratocumulus, nimbostratus, altostratus.
Heaped
Cumulus
Large heaped clouds, piled like cotton balls. They develop vertically, through several layers. Cumulus, cumulonimbus, altocumulus.

slides.label: Cloud abbreviations
slides.notes: Point out the pattern rather than asking them to memorise a list: nimbo or nimbus means rain-bearing, alto means middle, cirro means high. Cumulonimbus is the one to know cold - it means thunder.
slides.html:
Clouds
The ten abbreviations
You will see these on charts and in forecasts.
▸Cirrus — Ci
▸Cirrostratus — Cs
▸Cirrocumulus — Cc
▸Altocumulus — Ac
▸Altostratus — As
▸Nimbostratus — Ns
▸Cumulonimbus — Cb
▸Stratocumulus — Sc
▸Stratus — St
▸Cumulus — Cu

slides.label: Cloud patterns and heights
slides.notes: Leave this up while cadets copy it, or issue it as a handout. It is the reference sheet for the rest of the section.
slides.html:
Clouds
Patterns and heights

slides.label: Cross section exercise
slides.notes: Set the task before showing any of them, and hold the answers back. Work in pairs, two minutes per diagram, then take answers.
slides.html:
Exercise
Read these cross sections
Five diagrams coming up. For each one, work out the cloud types and the air movements.
▸What cloud is forming, and at what level?
▸Which way is the air moving?
▸Which front is this?
▸What would you see and feel on the ground?

slides.label: Approaching rain
slides.notes: Expect cirrus first, then thickening middle cloud, then nimbostratus and rain. This is a warm front approaching.
slides.html:
Exercise one
Approaching rain
What is coming, and how do you know?

slides.label: Depression cross section
slides.notes: They should identify warm front, warm sector, cold front in that order, and the anticlockwise circulation. Ask which part of the walk would be worst.
slides.html:
Exercise two
Depression cross section
Name the fronts and the sectors

slides.label: Warm front cross section
slides.notes: The shallow slope means the cloud sequence arrives hours ahead of the rain, and the rain is prolonged. That gives you warning if you are reading the sky.
slides.html:
Exercise three
Warm front cross section
A shallow slope — what does that mean for the rain?

slides.label: Cold front cross section
slides.notes: Steep front, towering cumulonimbus, short violent rain, then clearance and showers. Wind veers as it passes.
slides.html:
Exercise four
Cold front cross section
A steep slope — and a different kind of rain

slides.label: Occluded front cross section
slides.notes: The warm air is lifted clear of the ground entirely. Mixed and messy weather, and a sign the depression is filling.
slides.html:
Exercise five
Occluded front cross section
The cold front has caught the warm one

slides.label: Section: rising air
slides.notes: Signpost the shift from the synoptic scale to the local. This is the section that explains why the forecast was wrong for the valley you were actually in.
slides.html:
Part Four
Rising air and
local winds
The weather the chart does not show you — made by the ground under your feet.

slides.label: Dewpoint
slides.notes: The two lapse rates are the examinable numbers. The practical version is simpler: climb high enough and you walk into the cloud, which is exactly what hill fog is.
slides.html:
Rising air
Dewpoint
Cloud forms when invisible water vapour condenses into visible droplets or ice. For that, the air has to be saturated.
▸Air is cooled until it reaches its dew point — the temperature at which it can hold no more water.
▸As air rises it expands, because the pressure is lower. The energy used in expanding cools it.
▸Below the dewpoint — unsaturated — air cools at about 2°C per 200 m.
▸Above the dewpoint — saturated — it cools at about 1°C per 200 m.
▸So as warm air rises, its ability to hold vapour falls.
Rise, expand, cool, condense

slides.label: Sea breezes
slides.notes: Any cadet who has been on a beach knows the afternoon onshore breeze. Connect it to the line of cumulus that sits over the coast on a summer day.
slides.html:
Local winds
Sea breezes
The result of land and sea heating at different rates. They happen by day, when the land is warmer than the sea.
▸Warm air over the land cannot expand out over the sea, because that air is cooler and denser.
▸So it expands upwards instead.
▸Cumulus tends to form as that warm air rises over the land, to about 500 to 1500 metres.
By day, warm land air rises and cumulus forms

slides.label: Thermals
slides.notes: Glider pilots read thermals off the cumulus; walkers can read the same cloud as a sign of a hot afternoon and possible showers. Ask why cumulus forms in lines or clumps rather than evenly.
slides.html:
Local winds
Thermals
The sun warms the ground; the ground warms the air above it; bubbles of warm air rise.
▸Heated air expands and becomes less dense than the air around it.
▸The lighter air rises and cools, expanding into lower pressure as it climbs.
▸It stops rising when it has cooled to the temperature of the air around it.
▸Cumulus at the top of the thermal marks it — formed by the vapour in the rising air condensing.
Cumulus marks the top of the thermal

slides.label: Local warming
slides.notes: The gravity wind is why valleys are colder at night and why a still forecast can mean a persistent cold draught in a hollow. Relevant to choosing a campsite.
slides.html:
Local winds
Local warming and gravity winds
The thermal picture with the ground put back in.
▸The sun warms the ground; the air above it heats, expands and rises, making a thermal and its cumulus.
▸On one side, cool air rises up the hillside to fill the space left behind.
▸From the mountain tops comes a gravity wind — cold air flowing downslope because it is denser.
▸That cooler air reaches warmer ground, is heated in turn, and rises. The cycle keeps going.
Air rising up one slope, draining down another

slides.label: Air rising over mountains
slides.notes: The Pennines example makes it local and memorable. Practically: expect the cloud base on the up-wind side of the hill and a chance of clear ground once you are over the top.
slides.html:
Mountains
Air rising over high ground
An air mass moving from sea to land is forced up over the land barrier.
▸Rising, it cools. With enough moisture the vapour condenses at the dew point and cloud forms.
▸With hills and mountains, the cloud and the rain happen on the windward side.
▸On the leeward side the air descends fast, warms again, and the dewpoint rises.
▸Having lost moisture on the way up, the rain reduces or stops.
▸A local example: weather from the west rising over the Pennines gives Lancashire a higher average rainfall than Yorkshire.
Rain on the windward side, drier in the lee

slides.label: Funnels and eddies
slides.notes: The two-to-three-times figure is the one that changes decisions - a 25 mph forecast can be 60 mph on the ridge. Tie it to kit and to whether the route should stay high at all.
slides.html:
Mountains
Funnels and eddies
Wind on the tops is stronger than at ground level — often much stronger.
▸An air mass crossing flat land occupies a certain depth. Hitting a mountain, that depth is squeezed between the summit and the troposphere.
▸More air arriving means more air forced upwards, so the speed rises. The strongest wind is where it crosses the summit.
▸Wind at the top can be two to three times the valley speed — two to three times what the lowland forecast quoted.
▸That slows you down and makes it far colder than the thermometer says: wind chill.
▸Speeds increase through narrow passes, then spread out on the lee side, where the airflow can stay turbulent and erratic for some distance.
Squeezed over the summit, turbulent in the lee

slides.label: Banner clouds
slides.notes: Worth knowing because it is a visible sign of strong wind and turbulence on the lee side. If you can see a banner, the summit is windier than where you are standing.
slides.html:
Mountains
Banner clouds
A cloud that forms downwind of a crest or an isolated peak and streams from it like a flag.
▸Do not confuse it with snow blown off the summit and carried downwind.
▸Two mechanisms are thought to be involved.
▸Mainly a lee eddy, lifting air behind the peak above the condensation level.
▸A pressure reduction behind the obstacle would also help condensation — much as trails form at an aircraft wingtip.
A banner streaming from the peak

slides.label: Temperature inversion
slides.notes: This is the cloud inversion cadets see photographs of - valley fog with clear summits above. Practically it means the valley can be freezing and grey while the tops are sunny.
slides.html:
Mountains
Temperature inversion
Normally the troposphere gets colder as you climb. Sometimes a layer forms where it gets warmer instead.
▸Common in areas of high pressure, where air high up sinks towards the ground.
▸Sinking, it dries out and warms up.
▸That warm layer acts as a lid, trapping cooler air near the surface — warm air is more buoyant, so it floats above the cold.
▸Climb the mountain now and it gets warmer towards the top. Inverted from what you would expect.
Warm air lidding cold air in the valley

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Round the room. The four answers are polar maritime with frequent showers, anticlockwise and clockwise, wind strength, and two to three times. If they get the last one they will pack properly.
slides.html:
Learning Outcome 5
Can you answer these four?
1
Which air mass most often affects the British Isles, and what weather does it bring?
2
Which way does the wind blow round a low, and round a high?
3
What does isobar spacing tell you?
4
Wind at the summit is how many times the valley speed?
That completes Basic Navigation, LO1–LO5
